content: 1. Safe working conditions and appropriate remuneration for health workers must be implemented to ensure measurable improvements in access to healthcare professionals in rural and remote areas. 2. The need for updated guidelines was first highlighted in the WHO's 2010 recommendations on increasing access to health workers in remote and rural areas through improved retention. This revision is based on new evidence, research, and feedback from Member States. 3. The updated guideline comes at a critical time when global efforts are required to address a pandemic amidst a shortfall of 18 million health workers needed for universal health coverage. 4. The G-8 communiqué of July 2008 emphasized the importance of retaining health workers effectively, as outlined in the Tokyo Framework for Action on Global Health. 5. The WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel (2010) urged Member States to adopt measures to address the geographical maldistribution of health workers and support their retention in underserved areas through education, financial incentives, regulatory measures, and social and professional support. 6. The 2010 WHO guideline on increasing access to health workers in rural and remote areas was developed in response to global leaders, civil society, and Member States' requests. It provided 16 evidence-based recommendations for policymakers to design, implement, and evaluate strategies to attract and retain health workers in these areas. 7. The 2016 Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 aimed to optimize the performance, quality, and impact of the health workforce through evidence-informed policies, contributing to universal health coverage, resilience, and strengthened health systems. 8. The High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth (2016) recommended reforming service models to focus on high-quality, affordable, integrated, community-based, and people-centered primary and ambulatory care, particularly in underserved areas. 9. The primary audience for this guideline includes national authorities across various sectors such as health, finance, education, labor, and public service, responsible for policies affecting the health workforce. Secondary audiences include health service managers, educators, health workers, employers, regulatory bodies, civil society, NGOs, and rural communities. 10. Sustained political, institutional, and financial commitments are essential for improving rural health outcomes. Community participation and engagement are critical at all levels of planning and implementing retention strategies. 11. The guideline aims to support national authorities in strengthening the density and capacity of the health workforce in rural and remote areas, contributing to universal health coverage and sustainable development. 12. The recommendations focus on interventions within the scope of health workforce policy, planning, and management, categorized into education, regulation, incentives, and support. 13. The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the importance of equitable access to competent health workers, primary healthcare, and resilient health systems. The recommendations are increasingly relevant for emergency preparedness and response. 14. Policies to develop and increase equitable access to rural health workers are vital for building resilient health systems capable of addressing emergencies. 15. The guideline applies to all health worker occupations in the formal, regulated health sector, including students in health-related disciplines. It emphasizes the importance of considering the impact of policies on different health occupations and gender. 16. Rural and remote areas are defined based on national characteristics such as population size, density, and economic structures. Remote populations, often smaller and more isolated, face greater socioeconomic disadvantages and worse health outcomes. 17. The guideline highlights the need to engage with local communities to ensure effective planning and implementation of health workforce strategies in rural and remote areas. 18. The recommendations aim to increase the availability of motivated and skilled health workers in rural and remote areas through improved workforce development, attraction, recruitment, and retention. 19. The WHO Steering Group managed the guideline update process, involving evidence teams, methodologists, and external reviewers. The group will also oversee the dissemination and implementation of the guideline.
